stem: Which of these cells has cilia?

options.content: A root hair cell
options.rationale: A root hair is a single long extension of the cell, not cilia.

options.content: A red blood cell
options.rationale: Red blood cells have a smooth surface and no cilia.

options.content: A cell lining the trachea
options.rationale: Ciliated cells line the trachea and bronchi.

options.content: A palisade mesophyll cell
options.rationale: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts but have no cilia.

explanation: Ciliated cells line the airways (trachea and bronchi). Their cilia beat to sweep mucus, with trapped dust and bacteria, up towards the throat.

stem: Why is it an advantage for a red blood cell to have no nucleus?

options.content: It makes the cell heavier, so it sinks into the tissues.
options.rationale: Red blood cells stay in the blood vessels; weight is not the point.

options.content: It leaves more space for haemoglobin, so the cell can carry more oxygen.
options.rationale: More haemoglobin means more oxygen carried.

options.content: It allows the cell to divide more quickly.
options.rationale: Without a nucleus a red blood cell cannot divide at all.

options.content: It means the cell does not need oxygen.
options.rationale: The cell's job is to carry oxygen to other cells.

explanation: With no nucleus, the inside of a red blood cell can be filled with haemoglobin, the protein that combines with oxygen. More haemoglobin means more oxygen can be carried.

stem: A root hair cell has a long, thin extension. What is the main advantage of this?

options.content: It gives a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions.
options.rationale: More surface in contact with soil water means faster absorption.

options.content: It lets the cell photosynthesise in the soil.
options.rationale: There is no light in the soil, and root hair cells have no chloroplasts.

options.content: It stores starch for the plant.
options.rationale: Root hairs are for absorption, not storage.

options.content: It allows the cell to move through the soil.
options.rationale: Root hair cells do not move from place to place.

explanation: The root hair greatly increases the surface area of the cell in contact with soil water, so more water (by osmosis) and mineral ions (by active transport) are absorbed in a given time.

stem: Match each specialised cell with the feature that adapts it to its function.

right.content: Hair-like structures that beat to move mucus
A long extension that increases the surface area for absorption
A very long fibre that carries electrical impulses
A large food store and a jelly coat

explanation: Each cell's structure matches its job. The unused description (a large food store and a jelly coat) belongs to the egg cell.

stem: True or false: sperm cells contain many mitochondria, which release the energy needed for swimming.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. The mitochondria are packed into the middle section, just behind the head.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: sperm cells have many mitochondria to release energy from respiration for the beating flagellum.

explanation: A sperm swims by beating its flagellum, which needs energy. Many mitochondria in the middle section release this energy by aerobic respiration.

stem: True or false: a tissue is a group of organs working together.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. A tissue is a group of similar cells; a group of organs working together is an organ system.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. A tissue is a group of cells with similar structures that work together.

explanation: A tissue is a group of cells with similar structures working together. Tissues form organs, and organs working together form an organ system.

stem: Complete the levels of organisation, from smallest to largest.
explanation: Similar cells form a tissue; several tissues form an organ; organs with related functions form an organ system; organ systems make up the organism. An organelle is smaller than a cell.

stem: Which of these is an **organ**?

options.content: A palisade mesophyll cell
options.rationale: This is a single cell.

options.content: Xylem
options.rationale: Xylem is a tissue.

options.content: A leaf
options.rationale: A leaf is made of several tissues (epidermis, mesophyll, xylem, phloem) working together.

options.content: The shoot system
options.rationale: The shoot system is an organ system made of stems, leaves and flowers.

explanation: An organ is made of several different tissues working together. A leaf contains epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, so it is an organ.

stem: The wall of the stomach contains muscle tissue, glandular tissue and nervous tissue. What level of organisation is the stomach?

options.content: A tissue
options.rationale: It contains several different tissues.

options.content: An organ
options.rationale: Several tissues working together make an organ.

options.content: An organ system
options.rationale: The stomach is one part of the digestive system.

options.content: An organism
options.rationale: The stomach is only one part of the body.

explanation: The stomach is made of several different tissues working together, so it is an organ. It forms part of the digestive system (an organ system).
hints: How many different types of tissue does the stomach contain?

stem: Name the red protein in red blood cells that combines with oxygen.

rejected.feedback: Iron is part of haemoglobin, but the protein itself is haemoglobin.
Plasma is the liquid part of blood.

explanation: Haemoglobin is an iron-containing protein that fills red blood cells. It combines with oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.

stem: Name the part of a sperm cell that contains enzymes used to digest a way into the egg cell.

rejected.feedback: The nucleus carries the genetic material; the enzymes are in the acrosome.
The flagellum is used for swimming.

explanation: The acrosome is a sac at the tip of the sperm's head. It releases enzymes that digest the jelly coat around the egg, allowing the sperm to reach the egg's membrane.
hints: It is a sac at the very front of the sperm's head.

stem: What is the function of the jelly coat around an egg cell?

options.content: It provides food for the embryo.
options.rationale: Food (energy stores) is held in the egg's cytoplasm.

options.content: It helps the egg swim along the oviduct.
options.rationale: The egg cannot swim; it is moved by cilia in the oviduct.

options.content: It changes after fertilisation so that only one sperm can enter.
options.rationale: This prevents more than one sperm fertilising the egg.

options.content: It makes the enzymes that digest the sperm.
options.rationale: The sperm's acrosome releases enzymes; the jelly coat does not digest sperm.

explanation: After one sperm has entered, the jelly coat changes so that no more sperm can get in. This ensures the zygote has exactly the right number of chromosomes.
hints: What would happen if two sperm nuclei entered one egg?

stem: Which feature allows a phagocyte (a type of white blood cell) to engulf bacteria?

options.content: A flexible membrane and cytoplasm, so the cell can change shape and surround the bacteria
options.rationale: Phagocytes flow around bacteria and take them into the cell.

options.content: A rigid cell wall
options.rationale: White blood cells have no cell wall; a wall would prevent engulfing.

options.content: Haemoglobin
options.rationale: Haemoglobin is in red blood cells and carries oxygen.

options.content: A flagellum
options.rationale: Phagocytes move by changing shape, not with a flagellum.

explanation: Phagocytes have a flexible membrane and cytoplasm that let them change shape, flow around a bacterium and take it inside, where enzymes digest it (phagocytosis).
hints: To engulf a bacterium, the cell has to flow around it.

stem: Muscle cells contain very many mitochondria. Why?

options.content: To store oxygen for the muscle
options.rationale: Mitochondria do not store oxygen.

options.content: To make the protein filaments that contract
options.rationale: Proteins are made on ribosomes.

options.content: To carry out photosynthesis
options.rationale: Animal cells do not photosynthesise.

options.content: To release a lot of energy by respiration for contraction
options.rationale: Contraction needs a large supply of energy.

explanation: Muscle contraction uses a lot of energy. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, so muscle cells have many of them to release enough energy.
hints: Which organelle releases energy from glucose?

stem: A motor neurone carries impulses from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot. Its nerve fibre can be about a metre long.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the function of a neurone?

options.content: To carry oxygen around the body
options.rationale: That is the function of red blood cells.

options.content: To carry electrical impulses
options.rationale: Neurones conduct impulses from one part of the body to another.

options.content: To contract and cause movement
options.rationale: That is the function of muscle cells.

options.content: To engulf bacteria
options.rationale: That is the function of phagocytes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how **two** features of a neurone suit it to its function.

points.description: A very long fibre (axon) carries impulses over long distances, e.g. from the spinal cord to the foot
Many branched endings connect with many other neurones or with muscle cells / a fatty (myelin) sheath insulates the fibre and speeds up impulses

parts.explanation: The very long nerve fibre lets one cell carry an impulse all the way from the spinal cord to the foot. Its branched endings connect with many other cells, so impulses can be passed on to them; a fatty sheath around the fibre insulates it and speeds up the impulse.

explanation: Neurones carry electrical impulses. Their long fibres reach distant parts of the body, and their branched endings link them to many other cells.
hints: How far does this neurone have to carry its impulse?

stem: Red blood cells are biconcave discs, about 7.5 μm across, with no nucleus. Many capillaries are narrower than this.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the main advantage of the biconcave disc shape?

options.content: It stops the cell from bursting.
options.rationale: The shape is not about bursting.

options.content: It makes room for a nucleus.
options.rationale: Red blood cells have no nucleus.

options.content: It lets the cell swim through the plasma.
options.rationale: Red blood cells are carried along by the blood flow.

options.content: It gives a large surface area for oxygen to diffuse into and out of the cell.
options.rationale: A large surface area relative to volume speeds up diffusion.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: True or false: red blood cells are flexible, so they can squeeze through capillaries narrower than themselves.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Having no nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin, but it is also a disadvantage to a red blood cell. Suggest **one** disadvantage and explain it.

points.description: It has no DNA, so it cannot divide or make new proteins (to repair itself)
So it wears out and lives only a short time (about four months) / it must be replaced by new red blood cells made in the bone marrow

parts.explanation: Without a nucleus a red blood cell has no DNA, so it cannot divide or make new proteins to repair itself. It wears out after about four months and has to be replaced by new red blood cells made in the bone marrow.

explanation: The biconcave shape gives a large surface area for diffusion of oxygen, and flexibility lets the cells pass through narrow capillaries. Having no nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin, but it also means the cell cannot divide or repair itself, so red blood cells live only a few months and are constantly replaced.
hints: Think about surface area and diffusion.
What does a cell need its nucleus for?

stem: Describe how the structures of a sperm cell and an egg cell are adapted to their functions. [5]

points.description: Sperm: a flagellum (tail) for swimming to the egg
Sperm: many mitochondria to release energy for swimming
Sperm: acrosome containing enzymes to digest a way into the egg / through the jelly coat
Egg: large, with energy stores in the cytoplasm for the early embryo
Egg: jelly coat changes after fertilisation so only one sperm can enter
Both have a nucleus with half the number of chromosomes (haploid), so the zygote has the full number

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A sperm cell has a flagellum that it beats to swim towards the egg, and its middle section is packed with mitochondria that release energy for swimming. The acrosome in its head contains enzymes that digest a way through the jelly coat into the egg. An egg cell is much larger and contains energy stores in its cytoplasm, which supply the early embryo. Its jelly coat changes after one sperm has entered, so no other sperm can get in. Both cells have a nucleus with only half the usual number of chromosomes, so the zygote has the full number.
answerSpec.markingNotes: Any five points; at least one point about each cell for full marks.

explanation: Sperm are adapted for movement and penetration; eggs for providing food and allowing only one sperm in. Both carry half the chromosomes.
hints: Sperm must travel and get inside; eggs must feed the embryo and block extra sperm.

stem: The airways are lined with ciliated cells and cells that make mucus. What is the role of the cilia?

options.content: They trap dust and bacteria from the air.
options.rationale: The sticky mucus traps dust; the cilia move the mucus.

options.content: They absorb oxygen from the air.
options.rationale: Oxygen is absorbed in the alveoli, not by cilia.

options.content: They beat to sweep mucus, with trapped dust and bacteria, up away from the lungs.
options.rationale: The mucus is moved to the throat, where it is swallowed.

options.content: They kill bacteria with enzymes.
options.rationale: Cilia move mucus; they do not release enzymes.

explanation: Mucus traps dust and bacteria; the cilia beat in waves to sweep the mucus up the trachea to the throat, keeping the lungs clean.
hints: Which actually traps the dust: the cilia or the mucus?

stem: Which sequence is in the correct order, from the smallest level of organisation to the largest?

options.content: Leaf → palisade mesophyll → palisade cell → shoot system
options.rationale: This starts with an organ and puts the organ system last but the cell third.

options.content: Palisade cell → leaf → palisade mesophyll → shoot system
options.rationale: The leaf (an organ) is made of tissues such as palisade mesophyll, so the tissue comes first.

options.content: Palisade mesophyll → palisade cell → shoot system → leaf
options.rationale: The cell is the smallest level.

options.content: Palisade cell → palisade mesophyll → leaf → shoot system
options.rationale: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system.

explanation: Palisade cells (cells) form the palisade mesophyll (a tissue), which is part of a leaf (an organ), which is part of the shoot system (an organ system).
hints: Identify each item as a cell, tissue, organ or organ system first.

stem: Some cells in the stomach lining release large amounts of digestive enzymes, which are proteins. Which structures would you expect these cells to contain in large numbers?

options.content: Chloroplasts and ribosomes
options.rationale: Animal cells have no chloroplasts.

options.content: Ribosomes and mitochondria
options.rationale: Ribosomes make the protein enzymes; mitochondria release the energy needed to make them.

options.content: Cilia and a cell wall
options.rationale: Animal cells have no cell wall, and cilia move mucus rather than make enzymes.

options.content: Haemoglobin and a flagellum
options.rationale: These are features of red blood cells and sperm.

explanation: Enzymes are proteins, which are made on ribosomes. Making large amounts of protein needs a lot of energy, released by respiration in mitochondria.
hints: Where are proteins made in a cell?

stem: *Amoeba* is a single-celled organism that lives in pond water. Explain why *Amoeba* can survive without specialised cells, but a large organism such as a cow needs specialised cells, tissues and organs. [4]

points.description: *Amoeba* carries out all the life processes within its one cell
It is very small / has a large surface area to volume ratio, so substances diffuse in and out across its surface fast enough
In a cow most cells are far from the surface / it has a small surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion alone is too slow
Specialised cells, tissues and organs (e.g. lungs, heart and blood) carry out exchange and transport efficiently; division of labour

answerSpec.modelAnswer: *Amoeba* is a single cell that carries out every life process itself. Because it is so small, it has a large surface area compared with its volume, so oxygen, food and wastes can diffuse in and out across its surface fast enough. A cow is made of billions of cells, and most of them are far from the body surface, so diffusion alone would be far too slow. The cow therefore needs specialised cells organised into tissues and organs, such as the lungs to take in oxygen and the heart and blood to transport it, with each part doing one job very efficiently.

explanation: Small organisms can rely on diffusion across their surface; large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems built from specialised cells, tissues and organs.
hints: Compare how far substances must travel to reach the cells in each organism.
Think about surface area compared with volume.
